title: Sincerity of intention
hookLine: actions are by intentions (Bukhari), recalled from day 97
tomorrow: The heart as a lump of flesh

cards: Two travelers pack the same bags, take the same road, and arrive at the same city on the same day. From the outside, nothing tells them apart.

We met their story long ago, on day ninety-seven: the hadith that opens Sahih al-Bukhari. Actions are by intentions, and each person gets what they intended. One of them left home for Allah and His Messenger.
The other left for something in this world, some worldly gain or a marriage. The same move, and two completely different journeys.

teach.b: The word is ikhlas, sincerity: making something pure, clearing out whatever doesn't belong. The Qur'an uses the idea for religion itself.

In Pickthall's translation, people are commanded to serve Allah, "keeping religion pure for Him." And the short surah that declares Allah's oneness, say, He is Allah, the One, carries the name al-Ikhlas.
Pure oneness in belief, pure intention in action. A hadith in Sahih Muslim shows why teachers of the path take it seriously. It describes people brought for judgment who did impressive things.
One fought and died in battle. One learned and taught and recited the Qur'an. One gave generously.
Each is asked what he did, and each answers well.

teach.h: SO IT WOULD BE SAID. AND IT WAS.
teach.b: And each is told, in effect: you did it so that people would say you were brave, or learned, or generous, and it was said. The hadith ends hard for all three. But it isn't meant to make anyone afraid to do good.

teach.h: CHECK WHO THE DEED IS FOR.
teach.b: It's meant to make them check the label on the box. Ikhlas doesn't mean waiting for perfectly pure motives before you act. It means noticing, again and again, who the deed is for, and turning it back toward Allah.
Think back across this part: repentance, watchfulness, the evening ledger, detachment, patience, gratitude, reliance, contentment, love, fear and hope. Every one of them can be done for show.
Ikhlas is what keeps them real.

how: Muslims are taught to make their intention, niyyah, before acts of worship, and teachers of the inward path ask people to keep checking that their good deeds are done for Allah rather than for praise.

o: sincerity: doing a deed purely for Allah, not for show
a promise made aloud before witnesses in a mosque
reciting a surah perfectly, without a single mistake

s: ikhlas means you shouldn't act until your motives are perfectly pure
it means acting, and checking again and again who the deed is for.
in the hadith in Sahih Muslim, the generous man gave so people would call him generous
he gave so people would say it, and it was said.
the hadith judges the two emigrations by where they ended up
it judges each by what the person intended: each gets what they intended.

games.q: you're about to do something good, and you notice part of you wants the credit. what does ikhlas ask?
o: don't do it until your motives are pure.
do it, and turn the intention back toward Allah.
do it, and make sure people see.
games.why: the teachers of the path don't ask anyone to stop doing good. they ask you to keep checking who it's for, and to turn it back.

practice: Choose one good thing you plan to do soon, a post, a donation, a favor, a prayer, a hard day's work, and ask quietly: who is this for?
Let the honest answer come even if it's mixed, a bit for Allah, a bit for how it looks, and don't throw the deed away; just turn it, the way you'd turn a picture to face the right wall.
If you pray, say inside, this is for You; if you don't, say, this is for the good of it, not for the credit.

wordCard.voice: Ikhlas. Sincerity: clearing a deed of everything but the One it's for, and checking, again and again, who you're really doing it for. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: intention is everything. Same bags, same road, and a different journey inside. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 1905 (the fighter, the scholar and the generous man judged)
